title: Sandstorms of Arabia
summary: How winds such as the Shamal and haboobs lift sand and dust across Arabia, how sandstorms affect people and nature, and how to stay safe.
poll: Sandstorms do more harm than good.

versions.title: When the Sand Flies
versions.text:
The sky turns brown. A big wall of dust rolls in. It is a sandstorm!

In the desert, the ground gets hot. Hot air goes up. Then strong winds blow. They lift sand and dust off the ground.

One wind in Saudi Arabia is the Shamal. It blows from the north. It is strong in spring and in June and July. A storm cloud can blow dust, too. Its wind falls down and pushes a wall of dust. That is a haboob.

A grain of sand is heavy. It hops low on the ground. Dust is light. It goes up high. It can fly far, far away.

In a storm, you can not see well. Planes may have to wait. Cars must go slow. Dust can make it hard to breathe.

The camel is fine. It has long lashes. It can shut its nose. Dust that falls in the sea helps small sea plants grow.

How can you stay safe? Look for a warning on the news. Stay in. Shut the doors. Cover your nose and mouth. If you drive, slow down. Pull off the road if you can not see.

versions.text:
The sky slowly turns orange, then brown, as a huge wall of dust rolls toward the city. A sandstorm has arrived.

In the desert, the sun heats the ground strongly during the day. The hot air rises, and strong winds sweep across the open land. These winds lift loose sand and dust into the air.

One famous wind in Saudi Arabia is the Shamal, which means "north" in Arabic. It blows from the northwest and is usually strongest in spring and early summer. Thunderstorms can also create dust storms. Their cold winds rush down to the ground and push a tall wall of dust ahead of them. This kind of storm is called a haboob.

Sand and dust behave differently. A grain of sand is fairly heavy, so it bounces close to the ground. A dust particle is much lighter. It can rise high into the sky and travel hundreds of kilometers.

During a sandstorm, visibility drops, so people cannot see far. Flights may be delayed, and drivers must slow down. Dust in the air can also make it hard to breathe, especially for people with asthma.

Some living things are prepared for storms. Camels have long eyelashes and can close their nostrils. Dust that falls into the sea even carries iron, which helps tiny sea plants grow.

Weather experts forecast storms and send out warnings. When a storm comes, stay inside and close the windows. Cover your nose and mouth. Drivers should slow down and pull off the road if they cannot see.

versions.title: Sandstorms of Arabia: Walls of Wind and Dust
versions.text:
The sky gradually turns orange, then brown, as an enormous wall of dust rolls toward the city, swallowing buildings one after another, and residents realize that a sandstorm has arrived.

In the desert, the sun heats the ground intensely during the day, and the heated air rises while powerful winds sweep across the open landscape, lifting loose sand and dust into the atmosphere.

One famous wind in Saudi Arabia is the Shamal, whose name means "north" in Arabic. It blows from the northwest and is usually strongest in spring and early summer, when it can raise dust for several days at a time. Thunderstorms can also produce dust storms when their cold winds rush down to the ground and spread outward, pushing a towering wall of dust ahead of them, and this particular type of storm is called a haboob.

Sand and dust behave quite differently in the wind. A grain of sand is relatively heavy, so it bounces along close to the ground, while a dust particle is so light that it can rise kilometers into the sky and travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometers before it finally settles.

During a sandstorm, visibility can decrease so dramatically that people cannot see the end of their street. Flights may be delayed or redirected, and drivers must slow down considerably. Dust in the air can also make breathing difficult, especially for people with asthma.

Some living things show remarkable adaptation to these storms. Camels have long double rows of eyelashes and can close their nostrils to keep sand out, and for centuries desert travelers have similarly protected themselves by wrapping their head cloths across their faces. Dust that falls into the sea even delivers iron, a nutrient that helps microscopic plant-like organisms called phytoplankton grow.

Weather experts forecast storms and issue warnings using satellites, which can follow enormous dust clouds as they move across the region. When a storm approaches, stay inside and close the windows, and cover your nose and mouth with a mask or cloth. Drivers should slow down and pull off the road if they cannot see.

We should close all the windows so the dust and sand grains cannot blow into the house. We should also cover our nose and mouth so it is easier to breathe, since all that dust in the air can make breathing hard.

MID.prompt: Explain two different ways sandstorms affect people and one way they affect nature. Use details from the article.
checklist: I explained two effects on people.
I explained one effect on nature.
I used details from the article to support each point.
MID.modelAnswer: Sandstorms affect people in two main ways: they reduce visibility so badly that drivers cannot see the road and flights get delayed, and they also make breathing difficult, especially for people with asthma, because of all the tiny dust particles floating in the air. Winds like the Shamal, or sudden storms called a haboob, can arrive quickly, which is why weather experts forecast these storms so families can prepare in advance. Sandstorms also affect nature, since the dust that settles into the sea actually delivers iron that helps tiny plankton grow.

HIGH.prompt: Some people think sandstorms are only harmful. Using evidence from the article, explain whether you agree or disagree.
checklist: I clearly stated whether I agree or disagree.
I used at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my opinion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that sandstorms are only harmful, because the article shows they also bring real benefits even while causing serious problems. It is true that a sandstorm or haboob dramatically reduces visibility, delays flights, and makes breathing difficult for people with conditions like asthma, since dust particles fill the air. However, the same dust that falls into the sea delivers iron, an important nutrient that helps tiny plankton grow and supports the ocean food chain. Living things like camels also show a remarkable adaptation to these storms, since their long eyelashes and nostrils that can close let them survive conditions that would otherwise be dangerous, which suggests that the desert ecosystem has learned to live with, and even benefit from, the very storms that challenge it.
